section_title: Salt, Fire, and Peace with One Another

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 49 For everyone will be salted with fire. 50 Salt is good, but if the salt loses its saltiness, with what will you season it? Have salt among yourselves, and be at peace with one another.”

context_lines: Jesus closes the conversation with a short saying about everyone being salted with fire, followed by a warning about salt losing its saltiness. He ends with a direct command to have salt among themselves and live at peace with one another. This brings the conversation back to the disciples' dispute over greatness and their attempt to stop someone outside their circle.

The two images come together in Israel's offerings. [Leviticus 2:1–16](https://biblehub.com/bsb/leviticus/2.htm) describes burning a portion of the grain offering on the altar and requires salt with the offerings. Verse 13 calls it the salt of God's covenant. This provides a biblical background for reading Jesus' saying in terms of lives offered to God, although He does not explain each detail of the comparison here.

The [BSB footnote to verse 49](https://biblehub.com/bsb/mark/9.htm) records manuscripts that add an explicit statement about salting every sacrifice. The quotation above follows the shorter main text. The connection with Leviticus can be explored without adding the longer wording to it.

The final instruction is clear even where the imagery is debated: the disciples must retain the quality Jesus calls for and live together in peace. In the immediate setting, ambition and competition are the problems needing correction. The salt image should lead back to changed conduct toward one another, rather than becoming a puzzle detached from that concern.
common_interpretation_lines: There are different readings of the fire. [Calvin on Mark 9:49–50](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/calvin/mark/9.htm) connects the saying with offerings in Leviticus and understands believers as people purified and devoted to God through the gospel. The [USCCB note on verse 49](https://bible.usccb.org/bible/mark/9) likewise emphasizes purification and preservation in the disciples' spiritual life.

[Wesley](https://wesley.nnu.edu/john-wesley/john-wesleys-notes-on-the-bible/notes-on-the-gospel-according-to-st-mark/) takes the first fire as the continuing judgment just described, contrasting it with the grace that prepares believers as acceptable offerings. Within Free Grace teaching, [Charlie Bing](https://www.gracelife.org/resources/gracenotes/?id=18&lang=eng) instead connects the fire with judgment of everyone's works, with different outcomes for believers and unbelievers. These are commentary readings, rather than official rulings binding every member of a tradition. Despite their differences, they bring verse 50 back to lives shaped by God and peace within the community.
god_plan_lines: The offering background has a wider parallel in [Romans 12:1–5](https://biblehub.com/bsb/romans/12.htm). Because of God's mercy, believers are to offer their bodies as living sacrifices, let their minds be renewed, put pride aside, and recognize that they belong to one another in Christ. This does not settle every detail of Mark's fire image, but it shows how devotion to God and life together belong to the same calling.

Another biblical comparison is [1 Peter 1:3–9](https://biblehub.com/bsb/1_peter/1.htm): people given new birth through Christ's resurrection may suffer trials in which faith is tested like gold by fire. That is a supported parallel for the refining reading of this saying, rather than a claim that Peter is explaining Mark 9:49 directly.

Jesus later makes love for one another a mark by which His disciples will be recognized ([John 13:34–35](https://biblehub.com/bsb/john/13.htm)). The peace urged here serves that larger purpose: people shaped by His self-giving love are to make that love visible in their life together.
current_position_lines: We don't have a position on this passage yet. When our study reaches a conclusion the text supports, it will appear here.
